title: Lab 5 — Quiz 1
subtitle: Microscopy — resolution and types of microscopes

questions.prompt: Why is this microscope called a 'compound' microscope?

options.text: It uses both light and electrons
It can view live and dead specimens
It combines staining with magnification
It uses two sets of lenses: ocular and objective

questions.explanation: Compound = 2 sets of lenses (ocular lens for your eye, objective lens near the specimen). Light = white light. Brightfield = the field of view appears bright.

why.A: Compound light microscopes use only white light.
why.B: 'Compound' refers to the two lens sets.
why.C: Staining is separate from the name 'compound'.

options.text: How much larger the image appears
The ability to distinguish two separate objects
The difference in color between specimen and background
The diameter of the visible field

questions.explanation: Resolution is the ability to distinguish two separate objects — it reveals fine details for crisp, clear images.

questions.prompt: The left image is unstained and the right image is stained. What does staining add?

options.text: Magnification, making the cells appear larger in the field
Contrast, making cells easier to distinguish from the background
Life, so the cells can be viewed while they move around
Shorter wavelengths of light passing through the cells

questions.explanation: Staining with dyes creates contrast; without it, cells are hard to see against the background. Staining often kills cells and may distort their appearance.

why.C: Staining procedures often kill the cells.
why.D: Wavelength depends on the light source, not the stain.

questions.prompt: Which of these does NOT improve resolution on the brightfield microscope?

options.text: Adjusting the iris diaphragm under the stage
Using the 100X oil immersion lens with oil
Switching from the 100X lens back to the 40X lens
Adjusting the brightness dial near the switch

questions.explanation: Ways to improve resolution: adjust brightness, adjust the iris diaphragm, and use the oil immersion lens. (Never go back to 40X after using oil.)

why.A: The iris diaphragm controls light through the condenser and improves resolution.
why.B: Oil minimizes light scattering and improves resolution.
why.D: Brightness control is listed as a way to improve resolution.

questions.prompt: Why does immersion oil improve resolution with the 100X lens?

options.text: It magnifies the specimen another 10 times
It stains the bacteria so they're easier to see
Its high refractive index minimizes light scattering
It cools the lens so it can't crack

questions.explanation: Immersion oil has a high refractive index, minimizing light scattering so more light passes into the objective lens.

questions.prompt: Which type of microscopy produced this image of thin spirochetes glowing against a dark background?

options.text: Brightfield microscopy
Darkfield microscopy
Fluorescence microscopy
Transmission electron microscopy

questions.explanation: Darkfield scatters light so the specimen looks bright white against a dark background. It's used for Treponema pallidum, which is too thin for brightfield.

why.A: In brightfield, the background is bright.
why.D: TEM shows internal detail of thin slices in grayscale.

questions.prompt: Which microscope is best for viewing Treponema pallidum in a patient sample?

options.text: Brightfield
Scanning electron
Fluorescence with Auramine O
Darkfield

questions.explanation: T. pallidum doesn't grow well in culture and is too thin for brightfield, but is easily seen with darkfield.

why.A: T. pallidum is too thin to be seen with brightfield.
why.B: Electron microscopes require dead specimens and are expensive.

questions.prompt: These yellow glowing cells were stained with Auramine O. What type of microscopy is this, and what does the stain bind?

options.text: Darkfield microscopy; it binds endospores
Fluorescence microscopy; it binds acid-fast bacteria
Brightfield microscopy; it binds Gram-positive walls
Fluorescence microscopy; it binds viruses

questions.explanation: Fluorescence microscopes use short wavelengths (green, blue, UV) and glowing fluorochromes. Auramine O binds acid-fast bacteria.

why.A: Auramine O is a fluorochrome that binds acid-fast bacteria.

questions.prompt: This image shows rabies virus in brain tissue. How was the virus made visible?

options.text: A Gram stain viewed under brightfield
Scattered light under a darkfield microscope
Thin sections under a transmission electron microscope
Fluorochrome-tagged antibodies (fluorescence microscopy)

questions.explanation: Fluorochrome-tagged antibodies detect specific organisms in medical specimens — e.g., rabies virus in brain tissue.

why.A: Viruses aren't visualized by Gram staining.
why.C: This is a fluorescence image with tagged antibodies.

questions.prompt: Which type of microscopy produced this detailed 3-D view of external surface features?

options.text: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Darkfield microscopy
Brightfield microscopy

questions.explanation: SEM: electrons pass over the surface → detailed external features. Recall tip: Surface Electron Microscopy.

why.A: TEM shows internal features of thin slices.
why.C: Darkfield shows bright specimens on a dark field without surface detail.
why.D: Brightfield can't resolve surface detail like this.

questions.prompt: Which type of microscopy produced this image of internal structures in a thin slice?

options.text: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Fluorescence microscopy
Darkfield microscopy

questions.explanation: TEM: electrons pass through thin slices → detailed internal features. Recall tip: inTernal = TEM.

why.C: Fluorescence images glow on a dark background.

questions.prompt: What is the main trade-off of using an electron microscope?

options.text: Resolution is lower than with a light microscope
Only dead specimens can be visualized
Only live specimens can be visualized
Viruses are too small to be seen

questions.explanation: Electron microscopes give high-resolution images at high magnification, but only dead specimens can be viewed. They're expensive and not common.

why.A: Electron microscopes have much higher resolution.
why.D: Electron microscopes are excellent for viruses and prions.

questions.prompt: Why do electron microscopes have far greater resolution than light microscopes?

options.text: Electrons are larger than light waves
Electron microscopes use immersion oil
Electron microscopes use fluorochromes
Electrons have incredibly short wavelengths

questions.explanation: Shorter wavelengths squeeze between objects so they look separate. Electrons fit between atoms, pushing resolution far beyond light's limits.

why.A: Shorter wavelengths, not larger particles, improve resolution.
why.B: Oil is used with the 100X light lens.

questions.prompt: Fluorescence microscopes achieve higher resolution than standard brightfield because they use:

options.text: Longer wavelength light (red, infrared)
Beams of electrons
A dark background
Shorter wavelength light (green, blue, UV)

questions.explanation: Shorter wavelengths of light squeeze between objects more easily, helping them look separate.

why.C: A dark background is darkfield microscopy.

questions.prompt: Which statement about darkfield microscopy is FALSE?

options.text: The specimen looks bright against a dark background
Live, unstained specimens can be viewed
Intracellular details are clearly visible
It is used to see Treponema pallidum
It works by scattering light

questions.explanation: Darkfield's trade-off: intracellular details are NOT visible.

why.A: True — light is scattered by the specimen.
